title: Vision Transformers
blurb: Tests how ViT turns an image into a token sequence, the CLS token and positional embeddings, the inductive bias trade-off between CNNs and ViTs, why patch size matters, why transformers suit large-scale diffusion, and why the toy result doesn't overturn the data-hunger finding.

questions.prompt: How does a ViT turn an image into transformer input?
options: It runs a CNN first, then feeds the feature map to attention.
It cuts patches and projects each into an embedding.
It describes the image in words, then embeds the text.
It converts every pixel into its own token.
questions.explanation: Patches play the role of word tokens. The transformer itself is unchanged.

questions.prompt: What is the [CLS] token for in a ViT?
options: It stores the image's positional embeddings.
It is the first image patch, kept unmasked.
Its final output feeds the classifier.
It marks where each patch starts and ends.
questions.explanation: Borrowed from BERT, the learnable [CLS] token gathers information through attention and feeds the classifier.

questions.prompt: Which assumptions does a CNN build in that a ViT doesn't? Select all that apply.
options: Translation equivariance, since the same kernel applies everywhere
Colour matters more than shape
Every patch should attend to every other from layer one
Locality, since each kernel looks at a small neighbourhood
questions.explanation: The book names two: locality and translation equivariance. Full attention from the first layer is the ViT's design, the opposite of locality. Neither assumes colour beats shape.

questions.prompt: Why did ViT need large datasets or pretraining at ImageNet scale?
options: Its attention layers can't run on images smaller than 224 pixels.
It has fewer parameters than a CNN, so it underfits.
Transformers can't be trained with gradient descent on images.
With no built-in spatial assumptions, it had to learn them all from data.
questions.explanation: Freedom from assumptions means everything, even "nearby pixels relate", is learned, which costs data on complex, high-resolution images.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter think the ViT matched or beat the CNN on tiny digit images?
options: Tiny digits have little long-range structure.
ViTs always need less data than CNNs.
Digits are a sequence task, which favours transformers by design.
The CNN had a bug that capped its accuracy.
questions.explanation: A locality prior helps most where complex spatial structure is hard to discover. Scale up the images and the CNN's low-data edge should return.

questions.prompt: A 224 × 224 image is cut into 16 × 16 patches. How many patches is that?
Halving the patch size from 16 to 8 on a 224 × 224 image multiplies attention cost by what factor?
questions.explanation: Patches go from 196 to 784, four times as many. Attention is quadratic in sequence length, so cost grows 4² = 16 times.

questions.prompt: How does compute scale for self-attention against convolution as images grow?
options: Both grow linearly with image size.
Attention grows linearly. Convolution grows quadratically.
Attention grows quadratically, convolution linearly.
Neither depends on image size.
questions.explanation: That is why larger images or smaller patches make a ViT relatively more expensive than a CNN.

questions.prompt: What happens if a ViT has no positional encodings?
options: The model can't be trained at all.
It runs faster with no loss of information.
It behaves exactly like a CNN.
Shuffled patches give the same output.
questions.explanation: Self-attention is permutation-invariant. Positions must be added explicitly, while a CNN gets them from its structure.

questions.prompt: Listing 71.2 has 16 patches. How many positions does pos_embed cover?
questions.explanation: 16 patches plus 1 for the [CLS] token, so shape (1, 17, embed_dim).

questions.prompt: Why do large-scale diffusion models often use transformer denoisers (DiT)?
options: Transformers need less training data than U-Nets.
U-Nets can't produce images larger than 64 pixels.
At huge scale, flexibility beats a locality prior.
Transformers are the only networks that can predict noise.
questions.explanation: The same trade-off flips at scale: data-rich training lets a transformer learn long-range structure, so a built-in prior matters less.

questions.prompt: At 30 training examples, the ViT scored 0.276 and the CNN 0.102. What does this show?
options: The CNN can't learn from fewer than 100 examples.
Here the ViT won even with little data.
ViTs need less data than CNNs on every task.
Both models failed, so the comparison is meaningless.
questions.explanation: The result is scale- and task-specific. It doesn't overturn the ImageNet-scale finding that ViTs are data-hungry.

questions.prompt: What does Procedure 71.3 advise for a small dataset of simple, low-resolution images?
options: Always use a ViT, since it won the toy experiment.
Use neither, and fall back to hand-crafted features.
Test both a CNN and a ViT, since either can win.
Always use a CNN, since ViTs need huge data.
questions.explanation: The toy result shows the CNN's prior may not be needed, but on other tasks it may matter a lot. Only testing tells.

questions.prompt: Both "ViTs are always better" and "ViTs always need more data" are claims the chapter rejects. Why?
options: Both confuse ViTs with diffusion models.
Both depend on scale and task.
Both ignore that ViTs and CNNs have the same inductive bias.
Both were disproved at ImageNet scale.
questions.explanation: The same family needed massive data at ImageNet scale and won with 30 examples here. The trade-off is real and depends on the task.

bookExercises.prompt: Describe the two steps that turn an image into a transformer-compatible sequence (patch embedding, `[CLS]` token + positional embeddings), and state what changes about the transformer encoder itself to process this input.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Patch embedding (slice into fixed-size patches, flatten, linearly project each into a vector) and prepending a `[CLS]` token plus positional embeddings. Nothing about the transformer encoder itself changes. The exact same self-attention machinery from the transformers chapter is reused unmodified; only how the input sequence is constructed differs from a text transformer.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the two inductive-bias assumptions a CNN has that a ViT lacks, and state which one is responsible for a ViT's self-attention being permutation-invariant without positional encodings.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Locality (a kernel only looks at a small neighbourhood) and translation equivariance (the same kernel applied everywhere) are the two CNN assumptions a ViT lacks. The lack of any positional/locality structure is why a ViT's self-attention is permutation-invariant without positional encodings. Since every patch can attend to every other patch equally regardless of position, nothing in the raw attention mechanism distinguishes "patch 3 next to patch 4" from "patch 3 far from patch 12" unless positional information is explicitly added.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's data-scaling table (ViT beating CNN by a widening margin from n=30 to n=120), explain what "widening margin" suggests about how each architecture's sample efficiency scales with a small but growing amount of data, on this specific task.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The widening margin (ViT's advantage over CNN grows from 0.174 at n=30, to 0.158 at n=60, to 0.248 at n=120) suggests the ViT's sample efficiency on this specific task doesn't just match the CNN's. It improves faster as more data becomes available, at least across this small range. This is consistent with the ViT needing enough examples to learn the (simple, on this task) correlations that the CNN gets partially for free via its built-in bias, but once given even a modest amount of data, the ViT's greater flexibility lets it exploit that data at least as effectively, without a rigid architectural assumption limiting what it can represent.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's full-data result (CNN 0.8907 with 5,130 params vs. ViT 0.9333 with 18,154 params), explain why comparing final accuracy alone, without also noting the roughly 3.5x parameter-count difference, would give an incomplete picture of the trade-off between the two architectures on this task.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Reporting only final accuracy (0.8907 vs. 0.9333, a 4.3 percentage point gap) makes the ViT look like a clearly better choice, but the ViT achieves that with roughly 3.5x the parameters (18,154 vs. 5,130), a real cost in memory, inference compute, and (per Trade-offs) quadratic attention scaling if patch count grows. Whether that trade is worth it depends on the deployment context: for a resource-constrained setting, the CNN's slightly lower accuracy at less than a third of the parameter count could be the better overall choice, a trade-off the accuracy number alone doesn't convey.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague says "don't bother trying a ViT on our small dataset, everyone knows they need huge amounts of data." Using this chapter's Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say in response.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "This chapter's own measured result found the opposite on a small, low-resolution task. The ViT beat the CNN even at 30 training examples, and by a wider margin at 120. The 'ViTs need huge data' finding is real, but it's specifically documented at ImageNet scale with complex, high-resolution images with genuine long-range structure to learn; it's worth actually testing both architectures on our specific small dataset rather than assuming the folklore transfers, since whether the inductive bias trade-off favours one architecture depends on how much structure the task itself has."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 71.2 warns that forgetting positional encodings makes self-attention permutation-invariant. Describe concretely what would happen to a ViT's predictions on the SAME image with its patches randomly shuffled, if positional encodings were accidentally omitted.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Without positional encodings, shuffling an image's patches into a completely different spatial arrangement would produce the EXACT SAME prediction as the original, unshuffled image, because self-attention treats the input as an unordered set of tokens with no inherent notion of "where" each patch came from, so a shuffled image (which looks nothing like the original to a human, and would break a CNN's spatial understanding badly) would be computationally indistinguishable from the original image to a positional-encoding-free ViT.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about the original ViT paper's finding on pretraining dataset scale (JFT-300M vs. ImageNet-1k). Explain in your own words why the paper found ViT underperforming ResNet when pretrained on the smaller dataset, but outperforming it when pretrained on the much larger one, connecting this to this chapter's inductive-bias argument.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: When pretrained on the smaller ImageNet-1k dataset, ViT underperformed ResNet because ViT lacks any locality/translation-equivariance prior. Without enough data to learn "nearby pixels are usually related" from scratch, the ViT couldn't discover as useful a representation as the ResNet, which gets that structural knowledge built in for free regardless of dataset size. When pretrained on the much larger JFT-300M dataset, ViT outperformed ResNet because the larger dataset gave the ViT enough examples to learn spatial structure on its own, at which point its greater flexibility (no architectural constraint limiting what relationships it could represent) became an advantage rather than a data-hunger liability, exactly the same "the trade-off is scale-and-task-dependent, not universal" argument this chapter's own small-scale, low-complexity experiment demonstrates in the opposite direction.
